row.title: Who owns what you make
row.character_cast: Orbit opens, DiGi closes on whose it is
row.evidence_anchor: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (automatic copyright, fair dealing for named purposes, s.9(3) for computer generated work); UK government AI report, 18 March 2026
statutory_hooks: Education for a Connected World 2020, strand 8, copyright and ownership, ages 11 to 14
Computing programme of study, key stage 3 (create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts)
row.single_action_outcome: I can say who owns what I make, and use other people's work fairly.

slides.body: Whose is it, once you post it?
slides.title: Who owns what you make
slides.script: Read the title and the line under it, then stop. Orbit points the far too big magnifier at the question. No warning about trouble: nearly everyone here has made something worth owning.

lines: I'm Orbit. I like a question that needs checking.
You draw something, post it, and someone puts a chart song under it. Who owns what now?
One video, three owners. Today we check each one.
slides.script: Let Orbit land and say the lines. Then read the question on the wall once, in your own voice, and leave it hanging. Do not answer it. The class talks about it in a minute, before anyone is told anything.
slides.heading: Orbit

slides.why: You make things every week: photos, edits, drawings, videos. Most of what you were told about who owns them came from people guessing.
gains: One question to run on anything you make, use or post: whose is it?
The two questions UK law asks before you use someone else's work
What to write under anything you made with an AI tool
slides.script: Land the outcome as something they can do, not a rule they must follow. Point out the word made comes first: this lesson starts with what they own, and only then turns to what other people own. Read the first gain aloud, because whose is it? is the question the whole hour hangs on.
slides.outcome: I can say who owns what I make, and use other people's work fairly.

slides.prompt: In primary you learned: make it, credit it, ask first. A friend says that if you credit the band, you can put their whole song under a video you post. Right or wrong? Decide with your partner.
slides.script: Sixty seconds in pairs, then take three answers. This is retrieval from the primary lesson, so let them reach for make it, credit it, ask first on their own before you help. Do not correct anyone. Write the room's best guess on the board and say you will come back to it, because the answer is more interesting than either side expects.
slides.lookFor: Many will say right, or half right. Take the guesses and do not settle it yet, cycle two does. Listen for anyone who remembers that big public uses needed asking first, not only a credit.

words.meaning: The right to copy and share a work. It belongs to whoever made it, from the moment they make it.
Permission to use something you do not own, on the owner's terms.
The UK rule for using a small part of someone's work without asking, for named purposes only.

slides.script: Say each word and have the class say it back. Licence is the one most of them have never thought about, and it is the one that explains what happens when they post. Fair dealing will be new to almost everyone, which is useful, because it means nobody has a wrong version of it yet.
slides.heading: Three words for today

slides.body: Draw it, write it, film it or photograph it, and it is yours. There is no form, no stamp and no register to sign. UK law says the author is the person who creates the work, and copyright lasts until 70 years after that person dies. Your sketchbook is protected by the same law as a chart song.
slides.script: Say the last line slowly, because it surprises them. The UK Intellectual Property Office puts it plainly: you get copyright protection automatically, and there is not a register of copyright works in the UK. The law that says so is the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988. Nobody in this room needs to do anything to own what they made last night.
slides.heading: Yours the moment you make it

slides.script: Ten seconds of thinking time, then everyone shows one, two or three fingers on three. Most rooms get this one. It is here so every pupil says the rule once before the harder cases arrive, and so anyone who picked two or three hears it corrected without fuss.

options.text: Maya, from the moment she drew it
options.feedback: Yes. Copyright is automatic in the UK, so the drawing was hers the second it existed, shown to anyone or not.

options.text: Nobody yet, because she has not registered it
options.feedback: There is nothing to register. The UK has no register of copyright works, so ownership arrives with the drawing itself.

options.text: Nobody until she posts it with her name on it
options.feedback: Posting does not create ownership and a name does not either. She owned it before anyone saw it.

slides.question: Maya draws a fox in her sketchbook and never shows anyone. Who owns the copyright in the drawing?

slides.body: Maya posts the fox on TikTok. It is still hers. TikTok's UK terms say: "We don't own your content." Instagram's say: "We do not claim ownership." What posting does give them is a licence: permission to use it, worldwide, without paying her. On TikTok other users get a licence too, through Duet, Stitch and download.
slides.script: This is the part most adults get wrong in both directions. The app does not own your post, and you have still given something away. Keep the two halves together: you stay the owner, and the app gets permission. That is what the national framework means when it says controlling copyright of your own content may be limited on social media.
slides.heading: What posting gives the app

slides.prompt: Maya still owns her fox after she posts it. What has she given away, and to whom?
slides.script: Sixty seconds in pairs, then take three answers. Push for the word licence and for both parties: the app, and the other users. If a pupil says so posting is a bad idea, slow them down. Posting is a fine choice. It is a choice made better by knowing what it gives.
slides.lookFor: A licence. TikTok can use it worldwide without paying, and other users can Duet, Stitch and download it. She kept ownership and gave permission, which is why control over your own work on social media has limits.

slides.body: In the UK you may use part of someone's work without asking, but only for purposes the law names: quotation, criticism and review, caricature, parody or pastiche, and illustration for instruction. That is fair dealing. The UK has no general fair use. Fair use is American law, and the fair use pages on YouTube and Instagram are about American law.
slides.script: Expect pushback here, because they have heard fair use a hundred times from creators. Say it plainly: those creators may be right about the USA, and they are talking about a different country's law. The government's own report in March 2026 named the USA among countries with a general fair use, and the UK was not on that list.
slides.heading: Fair dealing, not fair use

steps.text: Quotation, review, parody and the rest of the short list. No named purpose, no fair dealing.
steps.title: First, a named purpose

steps.text: If people could have yours instead of theirs, it fails.
steps.title: Does it replace the original?

steps.text: Two lines to make a point is a quote. The whole thing is not.
steps.title: Did you take more than you needed?

slides.script: Point at each step as it builds. Watch me run it: a book review quotes two sentences and names the author. Purpose? Review, on the list. Would anyone read the review instead of the book? No. More than needed? No. Fair dealing. Then a harder one for the class: a whole film uploaded with one line of review on the end.
slides.caption: How would a fair minded, honest person have used it?
slides.heading: Two questions a fair person asks

slides.script: Ten seconds of thinking time, then fingers up on three: one, two or three. This is the it depends case done properly. There is no single verdict for every parody, and the right answer is the method rather than a ruling. Say that out loud, because pupils who want a clean yes or no need to hear that it depends is a real answer when you can say what it depends on.

options.text: Both questions: parody is a named purpose, not a free pass
options.feedback: Right. Parody gets him past the first gate. He still asks: does it replace the original, and is ten seconds more than he needed?

options.text: Nothing: parody is always allowed in the UK
options.feedback: Parody is a named purpose, and fair dealing still applies. The two questions do not switch off for a joke.

options.text: Nothing: parody is never allowed in the UK
options.feedback: Since 1 October 2014 parody has been a named purpose in UK law. It can be fair dealing if it passes the questions.

slides.question: Sam parodies a chart song's video with ten seconds of the original. What must he still check?

slides.body: Instagram's own help page lists what does not protect you when you post someone else's work: giving credit, adding a disclaimer, not making money from it, finding it online, and other people posting it too. So writing no copyright intended changes nothing. A credit tells people whose it is. Permission is the owner's yes.
slides.script: Go back to the board and the starter answer. Crediting the band was never enough for a whole song, and now they can see why in the platform's own words. Read the five items slowly, because at least one of them will be something a pupil has relied on. Keep it light: almost everyone has seen no copyright intended under a post and assumed it worked.
slides.heading: Credit is not permission

steps.text: YouTube can block the video, track it or monetise it.
steps.title: A Content ID claim

steps.text: Three strikes and the channel can be terminated. A strike expires after 90 days with Copyright School.
steps.title: A legal removal is a strike

steps.text: TikTok: infringing content may be removed and repeat infringers banned. Meta: content may be blocked, muted or removed.
steps.title: TikTok and Meta

slides.script: Walk the three steps one at a time and give them a moment to read each before you speak. The difference worth landing is between a claim and a strike: a claim is about one video, a strike counts towards losing the channel. Keep it as information rather than a threat. Nobody here is in trouble, and knowing the system is what lets them choose.
slides.caption: The platforms act on who owns the song, not on what your caption says.
slides.heading: What happens to a song under a video

slides.script: Ten seconds of thinking time, then fingers up: one, two or three. Option three is the one to head off, because frightened pupils hide things. A claim is about one video. Say that clearly and move on.

options.text: It can be blocked, tracked or monetised
options.feedback: Yes. A claim is about this one video. A strike is different: that comes with a legal removal, and three of them can end a channel.

options.text: Nothing, because you credited the band in the description
options.feedback: Credit is on Instagram's list of things that do not protect you, and Content ID reads the song, not the description.

options.text: Your whole channel is deleted straight away
options.feedback: A claim does not end a channel. Strikes come from legal removals, and it takes three for a channel to be at risk of termination.

slides.question: A Content ID claim lands on your YouTube video because of the song under it. What can happen to that video?

slides.body: A Creative Commons licence is a yes, written down before you ask. CC BY 4.0 lets you share and adapt the work as long as you give credit, link to the licence and say if you made changes. The credit has four parts, called TASL: Title, Author, Source, Licence.
slides.script: This is the primary habit of crediting carried up a level, and it is the good news in the lesson. Write an example on the board as you talk: Title, Harbour at dawn. Author, J. Okafor. Source, the link where you found it. Licence, CC BY 4.0. Make clear the names are made up for the example. Pupils will write their own TASL line in the practise.
slides.heading: Some makers say yes in advance

slides.body: UK law already has a rule for work made by a computer: the author is the person who made the arrangements for it to be made, and protection lasts 50 years. In March 2026 the government said the person writing the prompt will usually be the author. It also called the rule a legal contradiction that no court has tested, and proposed removing protection for work made wholly by a machine. That is a proposal. It is not law yet.
slides.script: Be exact here, because this is where the internet is loudest and least accurate. Three things are true at once: there is a rule today, the government thinks the rule does not hold together, and it has proposed a change that has not happened. The honest summary for a Year 8 is that the law is still being decided. Say that sentence and let it stand.
slides.heading: Made with AI. Whose is it?

slides.prompt: You type a prompt, pick one of four images, then paint over half of it by hand. Who should own it: you, the people who built the tool, or nobody?
slides.script: Ten seconds of quiet thinking first, then ninety seconds, whole class. Your job is referee. Push each claim one step: you typed eight words, is that making? You painted half of it, does that change things? If the room splits, say that the government's own report found the current rule hard to make sense of, so a split room is in good company. Then land the one thing that is settled.
slides.lookFor: Disagreement with reasons. The honest landing: today's rule points to whoever made the arrangements, the government says that will usually be the prompter, and it has proposed changing the rule for work made wholly by a machine. Nobody in the room has the final answer, the teacher included.

slides.script: Ten seconds of thinking time, then one, two or three fingers on three. This is the line that does not move while the law does: credit the tool and say what you did. Write it on the board under the starter answer and leave it there for the rest of the lesson.

options.text: The tool's name and what you did with it
options.feedback: That is the classroom rule. The law is still being decided, and saying how it was made is honest whichever way it goes.

options.text: Nothing, because nobody owns AI images
options.feedback: UK law has a rule for computer made work today, so nobody owns it is not what the law says. And honesty about how it was made is separate from ownership.

options.text: Your name alone, because you wrote the prompt
options.feedback: The government says the prompter will usually be the author, and authorship still does not make it hand made. Name the tool and say what you did.

slides.question: Your history homework includes an image you made with an AI tool. What should go under it?

slides.body: You do not need to register anything: your work is protected from the moment you make it. The choice that matters comes before you post. Posting gives the app a licence, and on TikTok other users can Duet, Stitch and download it. Post what you are happy to share on those terms. If someone posts your work as their own, you are the owner: report it to the platform and tell an adult you trust.
slides.script: This closes the circle back to cycle one, and it is the part they will use first. Keep it practical rather than anxious. Nothing here says do not post. It says post knowing the terms. If a pupil mentions their work being taken, take it seriously and quietly, and treat it as a conversation after the lesson rather than a case study in it.
slides.heading: Protecting what you make

config.prompt: Two breaths with Orbit: in as Orbit grows, out as Orbit shrinks. Then tell your neighbour one thing from today that surprised you, and write it on your sheet.
config.heading: Half time

slides.script: Half time. Two breaths with the whole room, in as Orbit grows and out as Orbit shrinks. Then thirty seconds in pairs on one thing that surprised them, and they write it on their sheet. Nothing is marked and nobody reads theirs out. Then straight into the sort.

config.label: Whose is it? · tap the class verdict

posts.why: You are the author from the first line. TikTok gets a licence to use it, and other users get one through Duet, Stitch and download, but TikTok's terms say it does not own your content.
posts.text: You draw a cartoon of your cat and post it on TikTok.

posts.why: CC BY is the maker's yes in advance, as long as you credit them, link the licence and say if you changed it. The TASL line does the credit.
posts.text: A photo under a CC BY licence goes in your project, with its Title, Author, Source and Licence written underneath.

posts.why: Criticism and review is a named purpose. Two lines do not replace the poem and are no more than you need. Name the poet.
posts.text: You quote two lines of a poem in your review of it, and name the poet.

posts.why: Instagram's own help page says giving credit and adding a disclaimer do not protect you. The photo is still theirs to share.
posts.text: You repost someone's photo with the caption: credit to them, no copyright intended.

posts.why: The whole song is more than any named purpose needs. Content ID can block, track or monetise the video, and a legal removal is a strike.
posts.text: You put a whole chart song under your YouTube video.

config.doneBody: Same five on the sheet now. This time every verdict needs its reason written next to it.

slides.script: Read each card, give the room ten seconds, take the vote by hands, tap the class verdict and read the why. Case four is the one to slow down on, because it is the habit most of them have seen everywhere. These five have clear answers, which is why they are here. Parody, memes and AI images are left out on purpose, and the next slide is where those go.
slides.caption: Sort the five together before the sheet.

slides.prompt: Two cases with no single verdict: a meme made from a stranger's photo, and an image you made with an AI tool and then edited. For each one, what would you need to know before you could decide?
slides.script: Ten seconds of quiet thinking first, then ninety seconds at tables. Do not let anyone settle on a verdict for every meme, because there is not one, and saying so is the accurate answer rather than a dodge. Take two tables' lists and put the best questions on the board next to the two from the diagram.
slides.lookFor: Meme: whose photo it is, whether it is for a named purpose such as parody or pastiche, whether it replaces the photo, and how much was taken. AI image: the law is still being decided, so credit the tool and say what you did. It depends, and here is what it depends on, is a full answer.

slides.body: Three credit lines on your sheet. One: a TASL credit for a Creative Commons photo. Two: a credit for two lines you quote in a review. Three: a line for an image you made with an AI tool, naming the tool and saying what you did.
slides.script: Five minutes, on their own. Circulate. The third line is the one to read over shoulders: it should name the tool and say what the pupil changed or chose, not only that a tool was used. Collect one strong example of each and read them out, with the pupil's permission and their name, because credit where it is due is the point.
slides.heading: Write the credit lines

slides.script: Exit check one, silent and solo. Ten seconds of thinking time, then fingers on three: one, two or three. If many pick two, the creators they watch have taught them a US rule, and that is worth five more minutes next lesson.

options.text: The UK has fair dealing for named purposes, with no general fair use
options.feedback: Correct. Fair use is American law. In the UK the use has to fit a named purpose and pass the two questions.

options.text: Fair use applies anywhere YouTube is available
options.feedback: YouTube's fair use page describes American law. The law that applies to a UK creator is UK law, and the UK has no general fair use.

options.text: Fair use applies if the clip is short enough
options.feedback: Length is part of the second question in fair dealing, did you take more than you needed. The UK has no fair use rule to apply.

slides.question: A creator says: it is fair use, so I can use the clip. They live and post in the UK. What is the UK position?

slides.script: Exit check two, silent and solo. Ten seconds of thinking time, then one, two or three fingers on three. This is the misconception the lesson exists to catch, so note anyone who picks two or three and give them the line from the board: credit is not permission.

options.text: Neither the credit nor the disclaimer protects her
options.feedback: Right. Giving credit and adding a disclaimer are both on Instagram's list of things that do not protect you. The photo is still the photographer's.

options.text: The credit protects her, because she named the photographer
options.feedback: Naming the photographer is good manners and it is still on Instagram's list of things that do not protect you. Credit is not permission.

options.text: The disclaimer protects her, because it shows she meant no harm
options.feedback: Meaning no harm does not change who owns the photo. A disclaimer is on Instagram's list of things that do not protect you.

slides.question: Jas reposts a photo with "all credit to the photographer, no copyright intended". What does Instagram's help page say?

points: You own what you make the moment you make it. Posting gives the app a licence, not ownership.
The UK has fair dealing for named purposes, not fair use. Does it replace the original? Did you take more than you needed?
Credit is not permission. Creative Commons is a yes in advance, and TASL is how you credit it.
With AI the law is still being decided. Credit the tool and say what you did.
slides.script: Four points, read by four pupils, one each. Do not add to them. Then point at the heading: whose is it? is the question that gets them to every one of the four.
slides.heading: Whose is it? Four things to keep

lines: I used to think a credit made anything fine. Good. That is one wrong answer we do not have to check again.
Your mission: before you post the next thing, ask whose is it?
If it is yours, post it knowing what the licence gives. If it is someone else's, find the yes: a named purpose, a Creative Commons licence, or the owner's own.
slides.script: The handover. Say nothing over it. Orbit owning a wrong answer is deliberate: checking is the habit, and being wrong once is how the habit starts. When the last line lands, ask them to say the mission back in their own words. The passport is next, then DiGi closes.
slides.heading: Orbit's mission for you

config.after: When the page is full, the big check earns Orbit's stamp.
config.prompt: Today filled part of the Making choices page. Tap to fill it in.
config.heading: The passport

slides.script: Thirty seconds, not a lecture. The passport is the record of getting ready for full access at sixteen, kept at home in the parents app, and every lesson here fills part of a page. Tap Fill the page, or let one of the class tap it. Say: when the page is full, the big check earns Orbit's stamp, and nobody can fail it. The parent note carries the home code that puts today in their own passport. The count on the wall is this screen's memory of your classes, not anyone's record.

lines: Everything you make is yours from the first line.
Everything you use was somebody else's first line.
Ask whose is it? before you post, and say what you did. That is the whole habit.
slides.script: Close on the third line and stop. It is the lesson in one sentence and it is the thing they will repeat to someone else. Do not add a warning after it.
slides.heading: One last thing

dsl_note.note: This lesson is about ownership rather than safeguarding, and carries no disclosure prompt. If a pupil says that pictures of themselves have been shared without their agreement, treat it as a safeguarding matter rather than a copyright one and follow your school policy.

questions.answer: Make it, credit it, ask first.
questions.question: In primary you learned a three part rule for using other people's work. Write the three parts.
questions.teaching_point: Retrieval from the primary lesson, My work and other people's work. Today takes the second and third parts further: what credit does not cover, and where the yes can come from.

questions.q: You draw a comic at home. When does it become yours?
questions.teaching_point: Copyright is automatic in the UK. Cycle one builds on this.

questions.q: Is crediting the maker the same as asking permission?
options: Yes, a credit counts as a yes
No, credit names them and permission is their yes
questions.teaching_point: The primary lesson separated the two. Today the platforms' own rules show why they stay separate.

questions.q: A friend makes a picture with an AI tool. What did primary say was always the honest move?
options: Say it was made with an AI tool
questions.teaching_point: Carried up today into the classroom rule: credit the tool and say what you did.

retrieval_starter.instructions: Four questions. Nobody marks these and nobody sees them but you.

parent_note.taught: Today we looked at who owns what your child makes. In the UK copyright is automatic, so their drawings, photos and writing are theirs from the moment they make them, and posting gives the app a licence rather than ownership. We also taught fair dealing, the UK's narrow rule for using other people's work, why crediting someone is not the same as permission, what happens to a song under a video, and the classroom rule for anything made with AI: credit the tool and say what you did.
parent_note.headline: What we taught today, and one thing to try at home
parent_note.passport: This lesson filled part of your teenager's passport page. The passport is the readiness record home and school build on the road to sixteen: skills proven at school, trust earned at home, each stage stamped when it is ready rather than when a birthday arrives. The skill proven today is saying who owns a piece of work and using other people's work fairly.
parent_note.try_this: Next time a video or post comes up at home, ask together: whose is it? Whose song, whose photo, whose words. It takes ten seconds, and there is often more than one owner in a single post.
parent_note.family_question: If you made a picture with an AI tool and then changed half of it by hand, whose would it be?

send.eal: Copyright, licence and fair dealing are the three words to pre teach, with the verdict labels Yours, Fine if you credit and Not yours to use on a card in first language on the desk. The five sort cases are short and concrete, and translate cleanly.
send.sensory: No sound is needed at any point, including the song case, which is described rather than played. The sort runs on paper or as three labelled corners if the board version is too busy for the room.
send.attention: Each teach slide carries one idea and is followed by a vote or a pair talk. The five sort cards can be handed out one at a time rather than as a set, and the credit lines task can be cut to two lines.
send.communication: Every sort case on the sheet carries the stem: whose is it? because. The credit lines task has a TASL frame with four labelled boxes, and nobody is required to speak to the whole room at any point.

lines: Made it yourself? It is yours. Posting gives a licence, not ownership.
Using someone else's? A named purpose, and does it replace theirs, and did you take more than you needed?
Made it with AI? Credit the tool and say what you did.

worksheet.title: Whose is it? Five cases, two it depends cases, and your own credit lines
worksheet.directions: For each case, choose the verdict and write the reason. For the two it depends cases, write what you would need to know. Finish with three credit lines of your own.

teacher_notes.teacher_tip: Do not let this turn into a lesson about getting into trouble. Open on what they own, because most of the room has made something worth owning, and keep the platform systems as facts to know rather than threats. Where the law is unsettled, say so plainly: the law is still being decided is the accurate answer, and a Year 8 class will respect it more than a confident guess.

questions.question: In primary you learned a three part rule for using other people's work. Write the three parts.
questions.teaching_point: Retrieval from the primary lesson, My work and other people's work. Today takes the second and third parts further: what credit does not cover, and where the yes can come from.

questions.q: You draw a comic at home. When does it become yours?
questions.teaching_point: Copyright is automatic in the UK. Cycle one builds on this.

questions.q: Is crediting the maker the same as asking permission?
options: Yes, a credit counts as a yes
No, credit names them and permission is their yes
questions.teaching_point: The primary lesson separated the two. Today the platforms' own rules show why they stay separate.

questions.q: A friend makes a picture with an AI tool. What did primary say was always the honest move?
options: Say it was made with an AI tool
questions.teaching_point: Carried up today into the classroom rule: credit the tool and say what you did.

starter_quiz.instructions: Four questions. Nobody marks these and nobody sees them but you.

evidence_base.claim: Copyright is automatic in the UK and there is no register of copyright works. The author is the person who creates the work, the owner has exclusive rights including to communicate the work to the public, and protection lasts 70 years after the author's death.
evidence_base.source: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, s.1(1), s.9(1), s.12(2), s.16; UK Intellectual Property Office, gov.uk/copyright

evidence_base.claim: Fair dealing covers named purposes only: quotation s.30(1ZA), criticism and review s.30(1), caricature, parody or pastiche s.30A (from 1 October 2014), illustration for instruction s.32. There is no statutory definition of fair dealing; the UK IPO asks how a fair minded and honest person would have dealt with the work, testing whether the use substitutes for the original and whether the amount was necessary.
evidence_base.source: CDPA 1988 s.30, s.30A, s.32; SI 2014/2356; UK IPO guidance on exceptions to copyright

evidence_base.claim: The UK has no general fair use. The government's March 2026 report names the USA among the countries with one, not the UK. YouTube's and Instagram's fair use pages describe US law.
evidence_base.source: CDPA 1988 s.28; UK government AI report, 18 March 2026

evidence_base.claim: YouTube Content ID claims can block, monetise or track a video; a legal removal is a copyright strike; three strikes and the channel can be terminated; strikes expire after 90 days with Copyright School.
evidence_base.source: YouTube Help, Content ID and copyright strikes

evidence_base.claim: TikTok: infringing content may be removed and repeat infringers banned. Meta: music content may be blocked, muted or removed. Instagram lists what does not protect you: giving credit, a disclaimer, not profiting, finding it online, others posting it too. TikTok's muting page could not be fetched and is not quoted.
evidence_base.source: TikTok Intellectual Property Policy; Meta music guidelines; Instagram Help Centre, copyright

evidence_base.claim: TikTok does not own users' content but posting grants it a worldwide, royalty free licence, and other users one through Duet, Stitch and download. Instagram does not claim ownership and takes a similar licence.
evidence_base.source: TikTok UK Terms of Service (July 2026), clause 4.9; Instagram Terms of Use

evidence_base.claim: For a computer generated work the author is the person by whom the arrangements necessary for its creation are undertaken, with 50 years of protection. The government's report says the prompter will usually be the author, calls s.9(3) a legal contradiction untested in court, and proposes removing protection for wholly machine made work. Not law yet.
evidence_base.source: CDPA 1988 s.9(3), s.12(7), s.178; UK government AI report, 18 March 2026

evidence_base.claim: CC BY 4.0 allows sharing and adapting with appropriate credit, a link to the licence, and an indication of changes. Credit is given by TASL: Title, Author, Source, Licence.
evidence_base.source: Creative Commons, CC BY 4.0 licence deed

evidence_base.claim: Strand 8, copyright and ownership, ages 11 to 14, has 11 statements including fair dealing, Creative Commons, protecting my own work, plagiarism, and why controlling copyright of my content may be limited when using social media. KS3 computing asks pupils to create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts with attention to trustworthiness.
evidence_base.source: UKCIS, Education for a Connected World 2020, page 45; DfE, Computing programme of study, key stage 3

hard_questions.answer: About the USA they may be right. Fair use is American law, and YouTube's and Instagram's fair use pages are about American law. In the UK the rule is fair dealing, for named purposes only, and there is no general fair use.
hard_questions.question: YouTubers say fair use all the time. Are they wrong?

hard_questions.answer: Because credit says whose it is and permission is their yes. Instagram's own help page lists giving credit among the things that do not protect you, along with a disclaimer, not making money, finding it online and other people posting it too.
hard_questions.question: If I credit the artist, why is that not enough?

hard_questions.answer: Today's UK rule says the person who made the arrangements for it to be made. The government says that will usually be the person writing the prompt, has called the rule a legal contradiction that no court has tested, and has proposed removing protection for work made wholly by a machine. That is not law yet. Until it is settled: credit the tool and say what you did.
hard_questions.question: So who owns my AI image?

hard_questions.answer: There is no single answer for every meme, and saying so is accurate. The photo in it has an owner. Parody, caricature and pastiche are named purposes, and the use still has to pass the two questions: does it replace the original, and did you take more than you needed.
hard_questions.question: Are memes illegal then?

hard_questions.answer: Other people posting it too is on Instagram's list of things that do not protect you. Each video is judged on its own, and the platforms act on who owns the song.
hard_questions.question: Everyone uses that song. How can it be wrong?

misconceptions: That crediting the maker, or writing no copyright intended, makes a repost fine. Instagram's own help page lists giving credit and a disclaimer among the things that do not protect you.
That the UK has fair use like the USA. It has fair dealing, for named purposes only, and the fair use pages on YouTube and Instagram describe American law.
That posting a picture hands ownership to the app. The app gets a licence and the pupil stays the owner.
That an AI image is either clearly yours or clearly nobody's. UK law has a rule for computer generated work, the government has proposed changing it, and no court has tested it.
That if it is online it is free to use. Finding it online is on Instagram's list of things that do not protect you.
teacher_notes.paper_fallback: Everything runs without screens. The five sort cases are on the sheet, the sort works as three corners of the room labelled Yours, Fine if you credit and Not yours to use, the two diagrams are on the sheet as numbered steps, and the credit lines are written by hand.
teacher_notes.commitment_stem: My commitment: before I post the next thing I made or used, I will ask whose is it, and the credit I will write is...

differentiation.stretch: Give the strongest pupils the parody case and ask them to write two versions of it, one that passes both fair dealing questions and one that fails one, then explain which question decided it and why.
differentiation.support: Keep the tool card with the three Whose is it? lines on the table throughout. Do sort cases one and four together using the stem: whose is it? because. Give the TASL frame with the four boxes already labelled.

prior_knowledge: From the KS2 lesson My work and other people's work: makers own their work the moment they make it, and credit is different from permission: make it, credit it, ask first.
From the KS2 lesson Stay the maker: the question of who made something when a computer helped make it.
From the KS3 lesson Is it doing my thinking?: using a tool is fine when you say that you used it.

worksheet_items.text: You draw a cartoon of your cat and post it on TikTok.
A photo under a CC BY licence goes in your project, with its Title, Author, Source and Licence written underneath.
You quote two lines of a poem in your review of it, and name the poet.
You repost someone's photo with the caption: credit to them, no copyright intended.
You put a whole chart song under your YouTube video.

worksheet_items.stem: Before I could decide, I would need to know...
worksheet_items.text: A meme made from a stranger's photo.

worksheet_items.stem: Before I could decide, I would need to know...
worksheet_items.text: An image you made with an AI tool and then edited by hand.
Three credit lines: a TASL credit for a Creative Commons photo, a credit for two lines quoted in a review, and a line for an AI image naming the tool and what you did.

parent_questions.answer: We taught what the platforms actually do rather than frightening anyone. On YouTube a Content ID claim can block, track or monetise one video; a strike comes from a legal removal, and three can end a channel. TikTok and Meta can remove or mute content. Knowing that lets your child choose, and credit alone does not protect them.
parent_questions.question: Is my child going to get into trouble for the songs in their videos?

parent_questions.answer: Your child does. Copyright is automatic in the UK, and TikTok's and Instagram's terms both say they do not own users' content. Posting does give the app a licence to use it, and on TikTok other users can Duet, Stitch and download it, which is worth talking about before something personal goes up.
parent_questions.question: Who owns the photos my child posts?

parent_questions.answer: No. We taught what the law says about AI made work, which is still being decided, and one honest rule for any time they do use it within the school's own rules: credit the tool and say what you did.
parent_questions.question: Are you teaching them to use AI for their homework?

subject_knowledge.body: Under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 the author is the person who creates the work, and the UK IPO says protection is automatic with no register. The owner's exclusive rights include communicating the work to the public, which is what posting a song under a video does. Protection lasts 70 years after the author dies.
subject_knowledge.heading: Copyright is automatic and belongs to the maker

subject_knowledge.body: Fair dealing covers named purposes: quotation, criticism and review, caricature, parody or pastiche (since 1 October 2014), and illustration for instruction. There is no statutory definition; the UK IPO asks how a fair minded and honest person would have dealt with the work, which comes down to whether the use substitutes for the original and whether the amount taken was necessary. The UK has no general fair use, and platform fair use pages describe US law.
subject_knowledge.heading: Fair dealing is narrow, and it is not fair use

subject_knowledge.body: YouTube Content ID claims can block, monetise or track; a legal removal is a strike; three strikes and a channel can be terminated; strikes expire after 90 days with Copyright School. TikTok says infringing content may be removed and repeat infringers banned. Meta says music content may be blocked, muted or removed. Instagram's help page lists what does not protect you: credit, a disclaimer, not profiting, finding it online, others posting it too.
subject_knowledge.heading: What the platforms do

subject_knowledge.body: Section 9(3) says the author of a computer generated work is the person who made the arrangements necessary for its creation, with 50 years of protection. The government's report of 18 March 2026 says the prompter will usually be the author, calls section 9(3) a legal contradiction untested in court, and proposes removing protection for wholly machine made work. It is a proposal, not law, and the lesson says so.
subject_knowledge.heading: AI made work: the law today and the proposal

subject_knowledge.body: Parody, memes and AI images are kept out of the verdict sort because none has a single clear verdict. They are taught as it depends, with the questions to decide by. A pupil who answers it depends and names what it depends on has given the accurate answer.
subject_knowledge.heading: What the lesson leaves unsettled, on purpose

teacher_notes.essential_question: Who owns what I make, remix or make with AI, and when can I use someone else's work?
teacher_notes.learning_objective: To say who owns a piece of work, and to use other people's work fairly under UK law and the platforms' own rules.
key_learning_points: Copyright in the UK is automatic and belongs to the person who made the work. Posting gives the app a licence, not ownership.
The UK has fair dealing for named purposes, not a general fair use. The two questions are whether it replaces the original and whether you took more than you needed.
Credit is not permission. Instagram's own help page says credit and disclaimers do not protect you.
Creative Commons is a yes in advance, credited with TASL: Title, Author, Source, Licence.
The law on AI made work is still being decided. The classroom rule is to credit the tool and say what you did.
